“One ruler from us and one ruler from you.”

The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“The rulers will come from us, and you will be the ministers.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The argument between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār grew so heated that open conflict almost broke out.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

According to the account, the situation was saved by one of the leaders of the Anṣār, Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ. He stepped forward and pledged allegiance to Abū Bakr as caliph. The Anṣār then accepted his decisive position.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Abū Bakr thus became the first of the four men who succeeded the Prophet and who later became known among Muslims as the “Rightly Guided Caliphs”: Abū Bakr of Banū Taym, then ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb of Banū ʿAdī, then ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān of Banū Umayya, and finally ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib of Banū Hāshim.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the struggle was not actually settled.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Banū Hāshim—the Prophet’s own family—had been absent from what happened at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida. When they learned what had taken place, they became angry. Some of them went to the place where the decision had been made.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One of them, ʿUtba ibn Abī Lahab, stood and recited poetry praising ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. His words amounted to putting ʿAlī forward as the only rightful candidate for the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The historian al-Yaʿqūbī, who died in 284 AH/897 CE, says that ʿAlī sent word to ʿUtba telling him to stop making this appeal.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But ʿAlī himself did not immediately pledge allegiance to Abū Bakr. A group from Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayya also held back.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

It also seems that some of those who were angry about what had happened went to ʿAlī intending to pledge allegiance to him instead. He told them to return the next day with their heads shaved. But when the next day came, only three men returned.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

It is true that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib later cooperated with the first caliph, Abū Bakr, and with the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. It is also true that the Anṣār accepted Abū ʿUbayda’s position because of the respect they had for him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the conflict itself remained beneath the surface.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At first it stayed hidden. Later it returned with great force, sometimes in bloody political conflict and sometimes in intellectual and ideological conflict.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The reasons behind it had never been resolved. Its underlying social and political content had not changed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Historically, however, this conflict played a positive role. First, it was a necessary part of the movement of social development. Second, it became a rich source of new intellectual movements. These movements later became part of the development of Arab-Islamic thought, especially its philosophical thought.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
4 — The Religious Form of the Conflict
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Although the struggle was driven by clear social and political interests, it eventually took a religious form. In that historical period, this was the form it naturally had to take.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The visible conflict therefore shifted. What had first appeared as a struggle between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār over political power became a struggle between the Hāshimites and the other groups over who possessed the religious right to the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This question of religious right opened another major dispute. It concerned the Islamic meaning of the caliphate itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Was the caliphate a right granted by God?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Was the office of caliph itself a purely divine office, like the Muslim understanding of prophethood and the prophet?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

If so, then God would have to choose the caliph personally, just as he chooses a prophet. The person chosen would have special qualities that made him fit to continue the Prophet’s mission. Above all, he would have to be the best and most knowledgeable of all people.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In this understanding, the caliph would also be the imam of the Muslims.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

God’s choice would be revealed to the Prophet, and the Prophet would then be required to announce that choice to the Muslims in clear and direct words. After the Prophet’s death, Muslims would have a religious duty to accept that choice and believe in it as part of faith itself, or as one of the foundations of belief, just as they believed in prophethood and the Prophet.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
On this view, the only difference between a prophet and an imam would be revelation: revelation belongs to the prophet, but not to the imam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Or was the caliphate simply a position of political leadership?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

If so, the caliph would not be chosen by God. The choice would belong to the Muslims themselves. They would decide how the caliph should be selected, and they would decide what qualities the person holding the office should possess.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Among those who rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office, another dispute then appeared.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Did the caliph have to come specifically from Banū Hāshim within Quraysh?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Did he only have to come from Quraysh in general?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Could he come from another Arab tribe outside Quraysh?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Or could any Muslim become caliph, whether Arab or non-Arab—even, as the Khārijites later said, “an Abyssinian slave”?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The view that the caliphate was a divine right was adopted by the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. It later became one of the basic principles of Shiʿi belief.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This required them to prove that God had revealed to the Prophet that ʿAlī had been chosen as imam of the Muslims, and that the Prophet himself had clearly announced this choice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They cite several reports in support of this position. The one on which they rely most heavily, and which has the strongest historical standing in the Islamic tradition, is the report known as the Hadith of Ghadīr.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The story is found in both Shiʿi and Sunni sources.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
According to these accounts, the Prophet was returning from Mecca to Medina after his final pilgrimage, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, when the following verse was revealed to him:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message.” (Qur’an, al-Māʾida 5:67)
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Prophet ordered his Companions to gather at a place beside a pool known as Ghadīr Khumm.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He then called ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib forward and had him stand on his right. The Prophet addressed the people and said:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

“I have been called to my Lord”—meaning that his death was near—“and I will answer that call. I am leaving this world and leaving among you two great trusts: the Book of God and my descendants, the people of my household.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He then took ʿAlī by the hand and raised it where everyone could see.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“People! Do I not have a greater claim over you than you have over yourselves?”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

“For whoever I am his mawlā, ʿAlī is his mawlā. O God, support whoever supports him, oppose whoever opposes him, give victory to whoever gives him victory, abandon whoever abandons him, and let the truth follow him wherever he goes.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
When the Prophet had finished speaking, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb congratulated ʿAlī:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Congratulations, ʿAlī. You have become my mawlā and the mawlā of every believing man and woman.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Prophet then returned to his tent and ordered another tent to be set up beside it for ʿAlī. He instructed the Muslims, men and women alike, to pledge allegiance to ʿAlī as imam and greet him as Commander of the Faithful.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As we have said, the different Islamic schools agree that the report itself has a historical basis. What they disagree about is what it means.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The disagreement centers on the word mawlā, and on the related idea of walāya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Shiʿis argue that the Prophet first used the word about himself when he said, “For whoever I am his mawlā.” Here, they say, the word means the person who holds religious authority over someone.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Prophet then immediately used the same word about ʿAlī:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The word must therefore carry the same meaning in both cases. On this reading, the Prophet appointed ʿAlī to exercise authority over the Muslims just as he himself had done. In other words, he appointed him their imam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿAlī could not, of course, become a prophet like Muhammad, because Islam holds that Muhammad was the final prophet and that no prophet would come after him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Other Muslim groups interpreted the word differently. They argued that mawlā, walāya, and the other forms of the same word used in the report refer only to friendship, loyalty, and affection. In their view, the report does not appoint ʿAlī to the imamate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This was one side of the religious dispute over the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Within the same debate, some Muslims argued that the Prophet had indirectly indicated that Abū Bakr should succeed him, rather than ʿAlī.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They pointed to the fact that during his final illness the Prophet ordered the Companions to perform the communal prayer with Abū Bakr leading them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They argued that leading the prayer was the “minor imamate,” and that this suggested that the Prophet also intended Abū Bakr to receive the “major imamate”—general leadership over Islam and the Muslim community.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used this argument when he called on people to pledge allegiance to Abū Bakr at the Saqīfa.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Another report used to support Abū Bakr’s claim was transmitted from Muhammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda. According to it, the Prophet once bought a camel from a man on credit.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Messenger of God, what if I return and do not find you?”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He meant: what if the Prophet had died?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Other reports of this kind are found in greater detail in collections of hadith and biographies of the Prophet.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The other main side of the dispute rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office at all. According to this view, it belonged to the Muslims themselves to choose whoever they believed was best suited to manage their affairs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Here a tribal problem appeared, and in some respects it may also have been a class problem.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We have already seen how both the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār claimed the right to the caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The issue had something close to a class dimension because, as we noted earlier, the Anṣār had developed something like class resentment toward the Muhājirūn. There was a clear difference between them, and the Muhājirūn had become the leading group within what we earlier called the Islamic communal order in Medina.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Other groups also entered the competition for supreme political leadership.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

When Abū Bakr became caliph at the meeting of the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida, for example, Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb—the father of Muʿāwiya, founder of the Umayyad state—refused at first to pledge allegiance to him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He accused the leaders of Quraysh, saying:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Are you satisfied, people of ʿAbd Manāf, to let someone outside your own group rule over you?”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The sources say that Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayya, despite their differences with one another, were both angry that a man from Banū Taym—Abū Bakr—had become caliph.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Was the caliphate restricted to Quraysh?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If so, did all of Quraysh have the right to it, or only Banū Hāshim?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Or did the right belong to all Muslims, Arabs and non-Arabs alike?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Throughout this conflict, the arguments took a religious form, and every side used religious evidence.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But in its substance and underlying content, the conflict was social and political, with something close to a class character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

On one side were wealthy merchants. On another were people hoping to gain wealth and expand their interests through the wars of conquest. Both could see control of the Islamic caliphate as a way of advancing the interests of their own social groups.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We have said that some Muslims rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They argued that the Prophet had left the matter to the Muslims themselves, who were to choose the person they thought best qualified to manage their common affairs.
